text.p: Tiny Luxembourg predicted a surplus when it set out its 1998 budget on Wednesday, in stark contrast to its European Union partners, notably France and Germany, which are struggling to meet the Maastricht single currency criteria.

Emphasising the healthy state of its finances, which guarantee it will qualify for Europe's planned economic and monetary union (EMU), Luxembourg said the surplus could be achieved despite a budgeted four percent rise in spending.
Budget Minister Marc Fischbach said Luxembourg's currently had a surplus of about 14 billion francs ($369.6 million). "We should be in surplus again in 1998," he added, giving no figure.
Fischbach estimated the 1997 surplus would be equal to about two percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
Countries taking part in EMU must have budget deficits below or close to three percent of GDP.
General government debt, including some taken on by the government from the CFL Luxembourg railway, was forecast at 7.7 percent of GDP in 1998 versus 7.5 percent in 1997.
Luxembourg's debt is the lowest of any EU nation.

"We have been very serious since the 1980's as far as our financial planning is concerned," said Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, adding that as a result, the Grand Duchy had not "entered into the game of debt and deficit".
Luxembourg budget spending is set by a "budgetary standard" or growth norm, which reflects the medium-term growth rate of GDP and is also linked to inflation.

For the 1998 budget, this was set at a little over four percent, taking total budget spending to 170.4 billion francs from 163.4 billion in 1997. Spending will be virtually balanced by receipts of 170.2 billion.
Real GDP growth for 1998 was forecast at 3.6 percent, unchnged from that forecast for 1997.
A package of income tax and ongoing company tax reductions, would cut 1998 revenues by seven billion and 3.7 billion francs respectively, Fischbach said.
The lowering of the corporate tax burden aims to boost growth and attract investment to Luxembourg.
Government income would be boosted by delayed taxes from the healthy profits made by banks between 1992 and 1994.
The full budget will be presented to parliament in September. ($ = 37.88 Luxembourg Francs)
